case_studies.title: Rehab Recovery Curve
case_studies.scenario: A physical therapist is studying the relationship between the number of weeks a patient has been in rehab (2 to 40 weeks) and their mobility score (0-100, higher is better). Recovery is fast early on and then plateaus - most of the improvement happens in the first 15 weeks, after which mobility scores level off with diminishing gains. The therapist also has two patients with unusually rapid early recovery (medical outliers) whose mobility scores jumped very early.
case_studies.question: Which correlation coefficient should the therapist use to summarize the strength of the relationship between weeks in rehab and mobility score?

options.text: Pearson correlation coefficient
options.explanation: Pearson assumes the relationship is linear and is sensitive to outliers. Since recovery here follows a diminishing-returns curve (fast early gains, then a plateau) rather than a straight line, and there are two outlier patients, Pearson's r will understate the true strength of the relationship and can be pulled around by the outliers.

options.text: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
options.explanation: Spearman correlates the ranks of the two variables rather than their raw values, so it captures any monotonic relationship - including the diminishing-returns curve here - without assuming linearity. It is also far less sensitive to the two outlier patients since it only cares about their rank, not their exact score.

options.text: Point-biserial correlation
options.explanation: Point-biserial correlation is designed for the case where one variable is continuous and the other is a true binary/dichotomous variable (e.g., treatment vs. no treatment). Weeks in rehab and mobility score are both continuous, so this does not apply here.

options.text: Phi coefficient
options.explanation: The phi coefficient measures association between two binary categorical variables. Neither weeks in rehab nor mobility score is binary, so this metric is not defined for this data.

case_studies.key_takeaway: When a relationship is monotonic but not a straight line, or when outliers are present, rank-based correlation (Spearman, or Kendall's tau for smaller samples) is usually a better summary than Pearson.
case_studies.common_misconception: Defaulting to Pearson's r as 'the' correlation coefficient without first checking (e.g., via a scatterplot) whether the relationship is actually linear.

experimentation.objective: Generate mobility-score data that follows a diminishing-returns curve with two added outliers, then compute Pearson and Spearman correlation on the same data and compare how differently they respond to the outliers.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

weeks = np.linspace(2, 40, 40)
# diminishing-returns recovery curve + noise
mobility = 100 * (1 - np.exp(-weeks / 10)) + rng.normal(0, 3, size=weeks.shape)

# two rapid-recovery outlier patients
weeks = np.append(weeks, [3, 5])
mobility = np.append(mobility, [95, 92])

# Try it yourself:
# from scipy.stats import pearsonr, spearmanr
# pearsonr(weeks, mobility)
# spearmanr(weeks, mobility)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compute Pearson and Spearman on the full data, then remove the two outlier patients and recompute Pearson only - see how much it shifts, while Spearman barely moves.

case_studies.title: The Fraud Model That Never Flags Fraud
case_studies.scenario: A bank builds a model to flag fraudulent transactions. Out of 100,000 transactions, only 400 (0.4%) are actually fraudulent. The team's first model reports 99.6% accuracy on the test set, and everyone is thrilled - until someone points out the model predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction.
case_studies.question: Which single metric would have caught this problem immediately, before anyone needed to inspect individual predictions?

options.text: Accuracy
options.explanation: This is exactly the metric that hid the problem. Because 99.6% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always predicts 'not fraud' still scores 99.6% accuracy - the metric is dominated by the majority class and says nothing about whether any fraud was ever caught.

options.text: Precision-Recall AUC
options.explanation: Precision-Recall AUC focuses specifically on how well the model finds the positive (fraud) class, which is what actually matters here. A model that never predicts fraud would have zero recall and a PR-AUC near the baseline fraud rate, immediately exposing the problem that accuracy hid.

options.text: ROC-AUC
options.explanation: ROC-AUC is a reasonable metric to also track, but with such extreme imbalance it can look deceptively good because the false-positive rate stays low even when recall on the tiny fraud class is poor - the large number of true negatives dominates. PR-AUC is more sensitive to performance specifically on the rare positive class.

options.text: Mean squared error (MSE)
options.explanation: MSE is an error metric for continuous/regression predictions. Fraud detection here is a classification problem (fraud vs. not fraud), so MSE is not the natural fit, and it would not have flagged the all-negative model's failure any more clearly than accuracy would.

case_studies.key_takeaway: For severely imbalanced classification, accuracy is close to meaningless - its value is dominated by the majority class. Metrics that isolate performance on the minority/positive class (PR-AUC, recall, F1 at a chosen threshold) are what actually reveal whether the model is doing its job.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating a single 'accuracy' number as sufficient evidence a classifier works, without checking the class distribution first.

experimentation.objective: Simulate a highly imbalanced fraud dataset, score a trivial 'always predict not-fraud' classifier, and compute accuracy vs. PR-AUC/recall side by side to see how differently they score the same (useless) model.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=100_000,
    n_features=10,
    weights=[0.996, 0.004],   # ~0.4% fraud, matches the scenario
    flip_y=0.01,
    random_state=42,
)

# Try it yourself:
# from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
# y_pred_naive = np.zeros_like(y)  # "always predict not-fraud"
# accuracy_score(y, y_pred_naive)
# average_precision_score(y, y_pred_naive)   # PR-AUC style score
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compute accuracy for the naive all-zero classifier, then compute recall and PR-AUC for the same predictions. Then try scoring a real (if simple) classifier trained on X, y and compare all metrics.

case_studies.title: Mansions Skewing the House-Price Model
case_studies.scenario: A real-estate analyst builds a regression model to predict house prices in a suburb where most homes sell between $200K and $500K. The dataset includes three multi-million-dollar mansions recently sold in the area. The analyst wants an error metric that reflects how good the model is for a 'typical' home, without letting the mansions dominate the score.
case_studies.question: Which metric best fits the analyst's goal?

options.text: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
options.explanation: MSE squares each residual, so an error on one of the multi-million-dollar mansions (likely large in absolute dollars) gets squared and can dominate the total, even if the model fits the typical $200K-$500K homes well. This works directly against the analyst's goal.

options.text: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
options.explanation: RMSE is just the square root of MSE, so it inherits the same sensitivity to squared residuals - a few large errors on the mansions still disproportionately drive the score up relative to how the model performs on typical homes.

options.text: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
options.explanation: MAE averages the absolute value of each residual instead of squaring it, so a large error on a mansion contributes proportionally rather than being amplified. This makes MAE a more faithful reflection of typical prediction error for the bulk of ordinary homes.

options.text: R-squared (R²)
options.explanation: R² measures the proportion of variance explained relative to a baseline (predicting the mean), not the typical size of the prediction error in dollars. It is also sensitive to the mansions in a different way: a few extreme values can inflate total variance and change R² without telling the analyst anything about typical-home accuracy.

case_studies.key_takeaway: MSE/RMSE penalize large errors quadratically, so they are the wrong choice when a few outliers should not dominate the evaluation. MAE treats every unit of error equally, which better reflects 'typical' performance.
case_studies.common_misconception: Reaching for RMSE by default because it is in the same units as the target, without checking whether outliers in the target variable will distort it.

experimentation.objective: Build a synthetic housing dataset with three extreme high-price outliers, evaluate the same model predictions with MSE/RMSE vs. MAE, and see how much the outliers move each one.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

n = 200
sqft = rng.normal(1800, 300, n)
price = 150 * sqft + rng.normal(0, 20000, n)   # typical homes, ~$200K-$500K

# add 3 mansion outliers
sqft = np.append(sqft, [9000, 10500, 12000])
price = np.append(price, [4_800_000, 5_500_000, 6_200_000])

# pretend model predictions (decent on typical homes, noticeably off on mansions)
y_pred = 150 * sqft + rng.normal(0, 20000, size=sqft.shape)

# Try it yourself:
# from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error
# rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(price, y_pred))
# mae = mean_absolute_error(price, y_pred)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compute RMSE and MAE on the full dataset, then recompute both after removing the 3 mansions, and compare how much each metric shifts.

case_studies.title: Comparing Recovery Time Across Two Small, Skewed Groups
case_studies.scenario: A clinical researcher compares recovery time (in days) between two independent groups of patients - 12 on a new drug, 12 on the standard treatment. A histogram of the pooled recovery times is strongly right-skewed (most patients recover quickly, a few take much longer), and each group has fewer than 15 patients.
case_studies.question: Which test is the most appropriate way to compare recovery time between the two groups?

options.text: Independent-samples t-test
options.explanation: The independent-samples t-test assumes the underlying data (or at least the sampling distribution of the mean) is approximately normal, and this assumption is most fragile with small samples. With only 12 patients per group and a strongly right-skewed distribution, the t-test's p-value cannot be trusted here.

options.text: Mann-Whitney U test
options.explanation: The Mann-Whitney U test compares the two groups based on ranks rather than raw values, so it does not require normality and is robust to the skew. It is designed exactly for comparing two independent groups with small or non-normal samples.

options.text: Paired t-test
options.explanation: A paired t-test is for two measurements taken on the same subjects (e.g., before/after), where each observation in one group is linked to a specific observation in the other. These are two independent groups of different patients, so there is no natural pairing to exploit.

options.text: Chi-square test of independence
options.explanation: Chi-square tests are for categorical data (comparing proportions/frequencies across categories), not continuous measurements like recovery time in days. Recovery time would need to be converted into categories to use this test, throwing away information the researcher already has.

case_studies.key_takeaway: When sample sizes are small and the data is visibly skewed, do not default to the t-test just because it is the most familiar comparison test - a rank-based non-parametric alternative like Mann-Whitney U is more appropriate when normality cannot be assumed.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming the Central Limit Theorem 'rescues' any comparison of means regardless of sample size - with n=12 per group, it does not reliably do so for a strongly skewed distribution.

experimentation.objective: Generate two independent right-skewed samples, run both a t-test and a Mann-Whitney U test on them, and compare the p-values - then repeat with much larger samples to see the tests converge.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

# right-skewed recovery times (days), small samples
group_new_drug = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=3.0, size=12)
group_standard = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=4.0, size=12)

# Try it yourself:
# from scipy.stats import ttest_ind, mannwhitneyu
# ttest_ind(group_new_drug, group_standard)
# mannwhitneyu(group_new_drug, group_standard)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Run both tests on the n=12 samples and compare p-values, then regenerate the same two groups with size=200 each and re-run both tests to see how much closer they agree at larger sample sizes.

case_studies.title: The Coefficient That Keeps Flipping Sign
case_studies.scenario: An agricultural scientist fits a linear regression predicting crop yield from rainfall, average temperature, and humidity. When she refits the model on slightly different bootstrap resamples of the same data, the coefficient for humidity flips from strongly positive to strongly negative across resamples, even though the model's overall predictions stay fairly stable. Rainfall and humidity are known to be closely related in this region.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely explanation for the unstable, sign-flipping humidity coefficient?

options.text: The model is overfitting because there are too many features relative to the sample size
options.explanation: Three predictors is a modest number of features, and overfitting from too many parameters usually shows up as unstable predictions on new data, not specifically as a coefficient flipping sign while overall predictions stay stable. That specific symptom points elsewhere.

options.text: Multicollinearity between rainfall and humidity is inflating the variance of their individual coefficient estimates
options.explanation: When two predictors are highly correlated, the regression has trouble attributing the shared effect to one variable versus the other - the individual coefficients become highly sensitive to small changes in the data (like a different bootstrap sample) even though the model's combined prediction stays stable. A sign-flipping coefficient alongside stable predictions is a classic multicollinearity signature.

options.text: The target variable (crop yield) needs a log transformation
options.explanation: A skewed target can cause other issues (like non-normal residuals or heteroscedasticity), but it does not specifically explain why one coefficient's sign becomes unstable across resamples while predictions stay consistent - that pattern points to a relationship between predictors, not the shape of the target.

options.text: The sample size is too small to estimate three coefficients reliably
options.explanation: If sample size alone were the issue, you would expect noisier estimates across the board, not a specific pattern involving two particular variables (rainfall and humidity) while predictions remain stable. The scientist needs to check the correlation between predictors specifically, not just add more data.

case_studies.key_takeaway: When individual coefficients are unstable but overall model predictions are not, check for multicollinearity (e.g., via a correlation matrix or variance inflation factor) before assuming the problem is sample size or model complexity.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating any instability in a model as generic 'overfitting' and reaching for regularization or more data, without diagnosing whether the actual cause is correlated predictors.

experimentation.objective: Generate rainfall and humidity as correlated variables, fit a regression across several bootstrap resamples, and watch the humidity coefficient's sign and magnitude shift.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

n = 60
rainfall = rng.normal(100, 15, n)
humidity = 0.85 * rainfall + rng.normal(0, 8, n)     # strongly correlated with rainfall
temperature = rng.normal(25, 3, n)

yield_ = (0.4 * rainfall + 0.1 * humidity + 0.6 * temperature
          + rng.normal(0, 5, n))

# Try it yourself:
# from numpy.linalg import lstsq
# X = np.column_stack([rainfall, humidity, temperature, np.ones(n)])
# for seed in range(5):
#     idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(n, n, replace=True)  # bootstrap resample
#     coef, *_ = lstsq(X[idx], yield_[idx], rcond=None)
#     print(coef)  # watch the humidity coefficient (2nd value) change sign/magnitude
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Run the bootstrap loop above and print the humidity coefficient each time. Then compute the correlation between rainfall and humidity directly, and compare a model with humidity dropped against the original three-variable model to see how little the predictions change.

case_studies.title: 99% Accuracy That Wasn't Real
case_studies.scenario: A student trains a decision tree with no depth limit on their entire dataset, achieves 99% accuracy, and reports this number as the model's performance in their project report. When the model is later run on new, unseen customer data in a demo, it performs barely better than random guessing.
case_studies.question: What evaluation step, if done before reporting the 99% number, would most likely have caught this problem?

options.text: Training a bigger, deeper tree to push accuracy even higher
options.explanation: This would likely make the problem worse, not better - an even deeper, more flexible tree memorizes the training data even further, which is precisely the failure mode already occurring here.

options.text: Evaluating the model on a held-out validation or test set the tree never saw during training
options.explanation: The 99% figure was measured on the exact data the tree was allowed to memorize, including its noise and idiosyncrasies - an unlimited-depth decision tree can essentially memorize the training set. A held-out set the model never saw would have exposed the gap between memorization and genuine generalization immediately.

options.text: Collecting more training data without changing the evaluation process
options.explanation: More data can help a model generalize better, but if the evaluation is still measured on data the model was trained on, the reported accuracy will still be optimistic and will not reveal the true generalization gap.

options.text: Removing all features and retraining
options.explanation: Removing all features would leave nothing for the tree to learn from at all. The issue here is not which features were used - it is that performance was measured on the same data used for training, which does not reveal the model's ability to generalize.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Any performance number measured on the same data a model was trained on should be treated as an upper bound on true performance, not a reliable estimate. A held-out validation/test set (or cross-validation) is the minimum bar for a trustworthy metric.
case_studies.common_misconception: Believing a high accuracy number is meaningful on its own, without asking what data it was measured against.

experimentation.objective: Train an unconstrained decision tree on a synthetic dataset, compare accuracy on the training set itself vs. a held-out test set, and see the gap directly.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=300, n_features=15, n_informative=4,
                            n_redundant=2, flip_y=0.15, random_state=5)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=5)

# Try it yourself:

experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compare train-set accuracy vs. test-set accuracy for the unconstrained tree, then set max_depth=3 and compare the same two numbers to see the gap shrink.

case_studies.title: The Hospital With the 'Worse' Mortality Rate
case_studies.scenario: A health-policy analyst compares two hospitals: Hospital A has a 6% overall patient mortality rate, and Hospital B has a 4% overall mortality rate. Based on this, a news article concludes Hospital B provides better care. However, Hospital A is a major trauma center that treats a much higher proportion of critically ill and high-risk patients than Hospital B.
case_studies.question: What should the analyst do before concluding that Hospital B provides better care?

options.text: Trust the raw mortality rates since both hospitals have large patient volumes
options.explanation: Large sample sizes make the raw percentages precise, but precision does not fix a comparison that ignores a major confounding variable. If Hospital A systematically treats sicker patients, its raw rate will look worse regardless of care quality, no matter how many patients are in each group.

options.text: Stratify the comparison by patient risk/severity level before comparing mortality rates
options.explanation: This is a textbook Simpson's Paradox setup: patient severity is a confounding variable that affects both which hospital a patient goes to and their likelihood of dying, regardless of care quality. Comparing mortality rate within similar severity bands (e.g., high-risk patients at A vs. high-risk patients at B) can reveal a very different - sometimes opposite - conclusion than the raw aggregate rates.

options.text: Compare only the average age of patients at each hospital
options.explanation: Age might be one relevant factor, but it is not necessarily the confounder driving the difference here - the scenario specifically flags patient severity/risk (trauma cases) as the key difference between the hospitals, not age specifically.

options.text: Increase the sample size at Hospital B to match Hospital A
options.explanation: The problem is not that Hospital B's estimate is imprecise due to a small sample - it is that the two raw rates are not comparing like with like. Collecting more of the same kind of patients at Hospital B would not address the mismatch in patient severity between the two hospitals.

case_studies.key_takeaway: A raw comparison between groups can reverse or disappear once you control for a variable that is related to both the grouping and the outcome. Always ask what could differ between groups besides the thing you are trying to measure.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating an aggregate statistic as automatically representative of every subgroup within it - this is the essence of Simpson's Paradox.

experimentation.objective: Build a synthetic dataset where a hospital's raw mortality rate looks worse only because of patient mix, then stratify by severity to see the conclusion reverse.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)

# Hospital A: mostly high-risk patients; Hospital B: mostly low-risk patients
hospital_a = pd.DataFrame({
    "severity": rng.choice(["high", "low"], size=1000, p=[0.7, 0.3]),
})
hospital_b = pd.DataFrame({
    "severity": rng.choice(["high", "low"], size=1000, p=[0.2, 0.8]),
})

# true mortality rates are actually BETTER at Hospital A within each severity group
mortality_rate = {"high": {"a": 0.10, "b": 0.14}, "low": {"a": 0.01, "b": 0.02}}

hospital_a["died"] = hospital_a["severity"].map(
    lambda s: rng.random() < mortality_rate[s]["a"])
hospital_b["died"] = hospital_b["severity"].map(
    lambda s: rng.random() < mortality_rate[s]["b"])

# Try it yourself:
# hospital_a["died"].mean(), hospital_b["died"].mean()          # raw rates
# hospital_a.groupby("severity")["died"].mean()                  # stratified
# hospital_b.groupby("severity")["died"].mean()
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compute the raw overall mortality rate for each hospital first, then group by severity and compare within each severity band - see the conclusion flip.

case_studies.title: Stopping the A/B Test Early
case_studies.scenario: A product team launches an A/B test comparing a new checkout button color, planned to run for 14 days to reach the pre-calculated sample size. On day 3, someone checks the p-value out of curiosity and sees p = 0.04. Excited, the team immediately stops the test and ships the new button as the winner.
case_studies.question: What is the main statistical problem with this decision?

options.text: Nothing is wrong - a p-value below 0.05 is a p-value below 0.05 regardless of when it is observed
options.explanation: The 0.05 threshold assumes you looked at the data once, at a pre-specified sample size. Checking repeatedly and stopping the moment the p-value crosses 0.05 changes the actual probability of a false positive - it is no longer 5%.

options.text: Repeatedly checking the p-value and stopping as soon as it looks significant inflates the true false-positive rate above the intended 5% (the 'peeking problem')
options.explanation: Random fluctuation alone will cause the p-value to dip below 0.05 at some point during a multi-day test a good portion of the time, purely by chance, even when there is no real effect. Stopping the instant that happens - rather than waiting for the pre-planned sample size - means the test is far more likely to declare a 'winner' that is actually noise.

options.text: The effect size of the button color change is too small to matter
options.explanation: This might or might not be true, but it is not the statistical flaw in the team's process - the problem is the decision rule (stop as soon as p < 0.05 is observed), which would inflate the false-positive rate even for a real, meaningful effect.

options.text: They should have used a chi-square test instead of whatever test produced the p-value
options.explanation: Swapping to a different test does not address the underlying issue. Any significance test used this way - checked repeatedly with stopping as soon as it crosses the threshold - suffers from the same inflated false-positive problem.

case_studies.key_takeaway: A p-value threshold is only valid at the sample size and check frequency it was designed for. Peeking at results and stopping early the moment they look favorable is one of the most common ways A/B tests generate false 'winners.'
case_studies.common_misconception: Believing p < 0.05 means the same thing regardless of how many times you checked or when you decided to stop looking.

experimentation.objective: Simulate many A/B tests where there is truly no difference between groups, checking the p-value daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05, and measure how often that produces a false 'significant' result compared to checking only once at the end.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

rng = np.random.default_rng(99)

def simulate_one_test(days=14, daily_n=50):
    # no real difference between groups -- same distribution for both
    group_a, group_b = [], []
    false_positive_from_peeking = False
    for day in range(1, days + 1):
        group_a.extend(rng.normal(0, 1, daily_n))
        group_b.extend(rng.normal(0, 1, daily_n))
        _, p = ttest_ind(group_a, group_b)
        if p < 0.05:
            false_positive_from_peeking = True
            break
    _, final_p = ttest_ind(group_a, group_b)
    return false_positive_from_peeking, final_p < 0.05

# Try it yourself:
# results = [simulate_one_test() for _ in range(500)]
# peeking_false_positive_rate = np.mean([r[0] for r in results])
# fixed_sample_false_positive_rate = np.mean([r[1] for r in results])
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Run the simulation across 500 fake experiments (where there is truly no effect) and compare the false-positive rate from 'peek and stop early' against the false-positive rate from waiting for the full 14 days.

case_studies.title: Segmenting a Curved Customer Cluster
case_studies.scenario: A marketing analyst wants to segment customers based on two behavioral features. A scatterplot of the data shows one dense, roughly circular blob of casual customers, and a second group of high-value customers forming a long, curved, sparser band running along the edge of the plot - plus a handful of clearly anomalous customers scattered far from both groups.
case_studies.question: Which clustering approach is best suited to this data?

options.text: K-means with k=2
options.explanation: K-means assumes clusters are roughly spherical and similar in density, and it assigns every point to some cluster. The curved, elongated band of high-value customers is not spherical, and K-means would likely split it unnaturally or blend it with the other group - and it would forcibly assign the anomalous customers to one of the two clusters instead of flagging them as unusual.

options.text: DBSCAN (density-based clustering)
options.explanation: DBSCAN groups points based on local density and does not assume any particular cluster shape, so it can follow the curved band of high-value customers as its own cluster while still separating the dense circular blob. It also naturally labels the scattered anomalous customers as noise/outliers instead of forcing them into a cluster.

options.text: Hierarchical clustering with complete linkage, cut into 2 clusters
options.explanation: Complete linkage tends to produce compact, roughly spherical clusters (similar bias to K-means) and struggles with elongated, curved shapes. It also has no built-in concept of 'noise' - the anomalous customers would be forced into whichever cluster is nearest, distorting the true segments.

options.text: Manually setting a fixed cluster count of 2 and assigning by nearest centroid
options.explanation: This describes essentially the same approach as K-means and inherits the same problems: it cannot represent a curved/elongated cluster shape well and has no mechanism for treating clear outliers separately from the two main groups.

case_studies.key_takeaway: The right clustering algorithm depends on the shape and density of the clusters in the data, not just how many groups you expect. Density-based methods like DBSCAN handle non-spherical shapes and noisy outliers far better than centroid-based methods like K-means.
case_studies.common_misconception: Reaching for K-means as the default clustering algorithm without first visualizing whether the data's clusters are actually spherical and similarly sized.

experimentation.objective: Generate a dataset with one circular blob, one curved/elongated cluster, and a few noise points, then cluster it with both K-means and DBSCAN and compare how each one handles the curved cluster and the outliers.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(15)

# dense circular blob
blob = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=0.5, size=(150, 2))

# curved band cluster (a noisy arc)
theta = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 150)
arc = np.column_stack([3 * np.cos(theta), 3 * np.sin(theta)]) + rng.normal(0, 0.15, (150, 2))
arc += [4, 0]

# a few anomalous/noise points scattered far away
noise = rng.uniform(-8, 8, size=(8, 2))

X = np.vstack([blob, arc, noise])

# Try it yourself:
# from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN

# dbscan_labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.6, min_samples=5).fit_predict(X)  # -1 = noise

case_studies.title: The Forecast That Looked Great Until It Wasn't
case_studies.scenario: A data scientist builds a model to predict next-month retail sales using historical monthly data spanning 5 years. They randomly shuffle all the rows and split 80% into training and 20% into a test set, using scikit-learn's default train_test_split. Cross-validated performance looks excellent - but when the model is deployed to actually forecast the next real month, its predictions are far worse than during testing.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely cause of the mismatch between test performance and real-world performance?

options.text: The model needs more features to forecast well in production
options.explanation: Adding features might help forecasting in general, but it does not explain the specific mismatch between a strong test score and poor real-world performance - that gap points to a flaw in how the test score was measured, not a lack of predictive signal.

options.text: Random shuffling before splitting let information from the future leak into the training set, inflating the test score (data leakage)
options.explanation: With time-ordered data, a random shuffle means some training examples come from months after some test examples. Sales trends, seasonality, and macro conditions carry over from month to month, so the model can effectively 'see the future' relative to some test points during training - something impossible in real deployment, where only the past is ever available. That is why the test score looked far better than real-world forecasting performance.

options.text: The model architecture is too simple for the data
options.explanation: A too-simple model would usually show up as mediocre performance on the test set itself, not as a large, specific gap between test performance and true forecast performance in deployment. The gap described here is a classic signature of information leaking across the train/test boundary, not underfitting.

options.text: The target variable should have been normalized before training
options.explanation: Normalization affects the scale the model trains on, but it would not explain why performance measured on a random shuffled split looks so much better than performance on genuinely future, unseen data - that specific pattern points to how the split itself was constructed.

case_studies.key_takeaway: For time-ordered data, a random train/test split can leak future information into training and produce a test score that does not reflect real forecasting ability. Always split chronologically (train on the past, test on a later period) for time series.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating train_test_split's default shuffling as safe for any dataset, without considering whether the rows have a time order that a model should not be allowed to see across.

experimentation.objective: Build a time-series dataset with a trend, compare performance from a random shuffled split vs. a chronological split, and see how much more optimistic the shuffled version looks.

case_studies.title: The 50-Layer Network That Won't Learn
case_studies.scenario: A researcher builds a very deep feedforward neural network (50 layers) using sigmoid activation functions throughout, following an older tutorial. After many epochs of training, the loss on the training set has barely moved from its initial value, even though the learning rate seems reasonable and the architecture has plenty of capacity.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely explanation for training barely progressing?

options.text: The learning rate is too low - just increase it
options.explanation: A low learning rate would produce slow but steady progress. Barely-moving loss across many epochs in a very deep sigmoid network is the signature of a different, structural problem: gradients shrinking as they propagate backward through many layers, not simply a small step size.

options.text: Vanishing gradients - sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so gradients shrink multiplicatively at each of the 50 layers during backpropagation, leaving almost nothing to update the early layers
options.explanation: Each layer's backward pass multiplies the incoming gradient by the local activation derivative. Sigmoid's derivative never exceeds 0.25 and is much smaller when the neuron is saturated, so across 50 layers the gradient reaching the earliest layers can shrink to nearly zero - those layers barely update, and the network stalls. Switching to a non-saturating activation like ReLU, or adding tools like batch normalization or residual connections, is the standard fix.

options.text: The model needs more training data
options.explanation: More data helps a model that is capacity- or generalization-limited, but it does not fix a gradient that is mathematically vanishing before it ever reaches the early layers - no amount of additional examples changes how much a layer's weights get updated per step.

options.text: The batch size needs to be larger
options.explanation: Batch size affects how noisy the gradient estimate is, not how much the gradient magnitude shrinks as it backpropagates through many saturating layers. A larger batch would still transmit an almost-zero gradient to the earliest layers in this setup.

case_studies.key_takeaway: In very deep networks, saturating activation functions like sigmoid or tanh can cause gradients to vanish as they backpropagate, effectively preventing early layers from learning. Non-saturating activations (ReLU and its variants), normalization layers, and skip/residual connections all exist largely to address this.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming stalled training always means the learning rate or amount of data is wrong, without considering whether the gradient is even reaching the earlier layers in meaningful size.

experimentation.objective: See directly why gradients shrink through many sigmoid layers by multiplying per-layer derivatives together, and compare it to what happens with ReLU's derivative instead.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def sigmoid_grad(x):
    s = sigmoid(x)
    return s * (1 - s)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_layers = 50
# assume pre-activations are moderately large (saturating the sigmoid),
# typical in deep nets without careful initialization
pre_activations = rng.normal(loc=3.0, scale=1.0, size=n_layers)

sigmoid_layer_grads = sigmoid_grad(pre_activations)
relu_layer_grads = (pre_activations > 0).astype(float)  # ReLU derivative: 1 if active, else 0

case_studies.title: Loss That Explodes Into NaN
case_studies.scenario: A team training a neural network sees the training loss decrease normally for the first few iterations, then suddenly spike, oscillate wildly, and eventually become NaN. Nothing about the data or architecture changed mid-training.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely cause, and what's the standard first fix to try?

options.text: The learning rate is too high, causing the optimizer to repeatedly overshoot the minimum until the weights diverge; reduce it
options.explanation: When the learning rate is too large relative to the curvature of the loss surface, each gradient step overshoots the minimum by more than the previous step undershot it, so the loss oscillates with growing amplitude rather than settling down - eventually producing values large enough to become NaN. Reducing the learning rate (or adding a warmup/decay schedule) is the standard first thing to check.

options.text: The model is overfitting to the training data
options.explanation: Overfitting shows up as training loss continuing to decrease while validation loss gets worse - it doesn't typically cause the training loss itself to spike, oscillate, and blow up to NaN. That specific pattern points to an optimization instability, not a generalization gap.

options.text: The network needs more layers to have enough capacity
options.explanation: Adding capacity doesn't address instability in the optimization process - it would if anything make an already-diverging training run more expensive without addressing why the loss is oscillating out of control in the first place.

options.text: The dataset is too small for the task
options.explanation: A too-small dataset can cause poor generalization or noisy gradient estimates, but the sudden spike-then-diverge pattern here is a hallmark of the step size being too large for the loss landscape's curvature, not a description of a small dataset's typical failure mode.

case_studies.key_takeaway: A loss that decreases initially and then spikes, oscillates, and diverges to NaN is a classic signature of too high a learning rate. It's usually the first hyperparameter to check before assuming something is wrong with the model or data.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating any bad training outcome as an architecture or data problem, without first checking whether the optimizer's step size is even appropriate for the loss surface.

experimentation.objective: Run simple gradient descent on a toy quadratic loss at two different learning rates and watch one converge smoothly while the other diverges.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

def loss(w):
    return (w - 3) ** 2   # simple convex loss, minimum at w=3

def grad(w):
    return 2 * (w - 3)

def run_gradient_descent(lr, steps=15, w0=0.0):
    w = w0
    history = [w]
    for _ in range(steps):
        w = w - lr * grad(w)
        history.append(w)
    return history

# Try it yourself:
# stable_history = run_gradient_descent(lr=0.1)
# unstable_history = run_gradient_descent(lr=1.1)   # too high for this loss curvature
# print(stable_history)
# print(unstable_history)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Run run_gradient_descent with lr=0.1 and lr=1.1 and print both histories - watch the second one grow in magnitude with each step instead of settling near w=3. Try a few learning rates in between to find roughly where the behavior flips.

case_studies.title: Classifying Digits With the Wrong Loss Function
case_studies.scenario: A student builds a neural network to classify handwritten digits (10 classes) with a softmax output layer, but trains it using mean squared error (MSE) loss between the predicted probability vector and a one-hot encoded label, instead of cross-entropy loss. Training is much slower to converge than expected, and predictions stay unconfident even after many epochs.
case_studies.question: What change would most directly address this training behavior?

options.text: Switch the loss function to categorical cross-entropy, the standard pairing for a softmax classification output
options.explanation: Cross-entropy's gradient with respect to the pre-softmax activations simplifies to (predicted probability - true label), which stays large whenever the prediction is confidently wrong and only shrinks as the prediction becomes correct. MSE combined with a saturating softmax output can produce a much smaller gradient exactly when the model is most wrong, slowing learning in precisely the cases that need the biggest correction.

options.text: Add more convolutional layers to the network
options.explanation: More capacity doesn't fix a mismatched loss function - the slow, unconfident convergence described here is a direct consequence of the loss/output combination, and a bigger model trained with the same loss would likely show the same sluggish behavior.

options.text: Increase the number of training epochs substantially
options.explanation: Training longer might eventually make some progress, but it's treating the symptom rather than the cause - the underlying issue is that the loss's gradient is small exactly when it should be large (a confidently wrong prediction), which more epochs alone doesn't fix efficiently.

options.text: Use a larger learning rate
options.explanation: A larger learning rate multiplies an already-too-small gradient by a bigger number, which can help a little, but it doesn't address why the gradient is small in the first place, and risks introducing training instability without fixing the fundamental mismatch.

case_studies.key_takeaway: The choice of loss function should match the task and output activation. Cross-entropy paired with softmax/sigmoid outputs produces a gradient that scales naturally with how wrong the prediction is; MSE paired with a saturating output activation can produce misleadingly small gradients precisely when the model is most wrong.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating MSE as a safe, generic default loss for any task, without considering how it interacts with the output layer's activation function for classification.

experimentation.objective: Compare the gradient produced by MSE vs. cross-entropy loss for the exact same confidently-wrong prediction, and see which one actually pushes the model to correct itself.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# a confidently wrong prediction: true label = 1, but pre-activation z is very negative
z = -8.0
y_true = 1.0
p = sigmoid(z)  # predicted probability, will be close to 0 (confidently wrong)

# gradient of MSE loss w.r.t. z:  dL/dz = (p - y_true) * p * (1 - p)
mse_grad = (p - y_true) * p * (1 - p)

# gradient of cross-entropy loss w.r.t. z:  dL/dz = (p - y_true)
cross_entropy_grad = (p - y_true)

# Try it yourself:
# print("predicted probability:", p)
# print("MSE gradient:", mse_grad)
# print("Cross-entropy gradient:", cross_entropy_grad)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Run the code with z = -8.0 (confidently wrong) and compare mse_grad to cross_entropy_grad. Then try z = 0.0 (an uncertain prediction) and see how the two gradients compare in that case instead.

case_studies.title: The CNN That Memorized 500 Images
case_studies.scenario: A team trains an image classification CNN from scratch on a small dataset - about 500 images per class, no data augmentation, no dropout. After training, accuracy on the training set reaches nearly 100%, but accuracy on a held-out validation set is far lower, and validation loss actually starts increasing partway through training while training loss keeps falling.
case_studies.question: Which single change would most directly help close this train/validation gap?

options.text: Add more convolutional layers to increase the model's capacity
options.explanation: This scenario already shows the model has more than enough capacity to fit the training data almost perfectly - adding more capacity would likely make memorization (and the gap) worse, not better.

options.text: Add data augmentation (and/or regularization like dropout) so the effective diversity of the small training set increases
options.explanation: With only 500 images per class and no augmentation, the network can effectively memorize the exact training images rather than learning generalizable features. Data augmentation (random crops, flips, color jitter, etc.) manufactures more varied training examples from the same images, and dropout/regularization discourages over-reliance on specific memorized patterns - both directly target the gap between train and validation performance.

options.text: Increase the learning rate
options.explanation: Learning rate affects how quickly the model reaches wherever it's heading during training - it doesn't address why the model is memorizing the training set rather than generalizing, so it wouldn't close the train/validation gap.

options.text: Train for many more epochs without any other changes
options.explanation: The validation loss is already increasing partway through training while training loss keeps falling - this is the network overfitting further with each additional epoch. Training longer without changing anything else would widen the gap, not close it.

case_studies.key_takeaway: A large, widening gap between training and validation performance on a small dataset is a classic overfitting signature. Data augmentation and regularization directly counter it by effectively increasing the diversity the model has to generalize across, rather than by changing model capacity or training duration.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming a deep learning model's problems are usually solved by adding more layers or training longer, when a small, unaugmented dataset is often the actual bottleneck.

experimentation.objective: Train a small neural network on a deliberately small synthetic dataset, then compare validation accuracy with and without a simple augmentation (noisy duplicates of the training examples).
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

case_studies.title: Is the Bounding Box Actually Right?
case_studies.scenario: A team evaluating an object-detection model reports 'classification accuracy': for each image, they check only whether the predicted class label matches the true object class, ignoring where exactly the predicted bounding box was drawn. Two sample predictions both get marked correct under this scheme - one where the predicted box tightly matches the true object's location, and another where the predicted box only barely overlaps the true object's corner.
case_studies.question: What's the problem with using plain classification accuracy to evaluate this object detector, and what's the standard alternative?

options.text: Nothing is wrong - if the class label is right, the detection should count as correct
options.explanation: This is exactly the blind spot the scenario is pointing at: a detector that finds the right class but draws the box almost anywhere still gets marked 'correct' under this scheme, even though it's barely locating the object. For most real uses of object detection, where the box is drawn matters as much as what's in it.

options.text: Mean Average Precision (mAP), which requires a predicted box to overlap the ground-truth box by at least some IoU threshold before counting it as a correct detection, better reflects real detection quality
options.explanation: mAP incorporates both whether the class is right and whether the box's location is accurate enough (via an Intersection-over-Union threshold, commonly 0.5) to count as a true positive. This directly distinguishes a tight, accurate box from one that barely overlaps the object, which plain classification accuracy cannot do.

options.text: Use mean squared error on the box coordinates only, ignoring the class prediction entirely
options.explanation: This drops the classification signal entirely, which is just as incomplete in the other direction - a detector needs to be evaluated on both getting the class right and localizing it well, which is exactly what mAP with an IoU threshold combines.

options.text: Use R-squared on the predicted confidence scores
options.explanation: R² measures how well a continuous prediction matches a continuous target on average - it isn't designed to evaluate discrete detection events (right class, right location) and wouldn't capture the localization quality the scenario is asking about.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Classification accuracy alone doesn't capture localization quality. Object detection evaluation needs a metric like mAP that combines correct classification with a localization threshold (IoU), so a right-class-wrong-location prediction isn't scored the same as a right-class-right-location one.
case_studies.common_misconception: Reusing a plain classification metric for a task (detection/localization) that has an extra dimension - where something is - that the metric was never designed to capture.

experimentation.objective: Compute Intersection-over-Union for a tight prediction vs. a barely-overlapping prediction against the same ground-truth box, and see how an IoU-thresholded detection criterion tells them apart when plain classification accuracy wouldn't.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

def iou(box_a, box_b):
    # box format: (x1, y1, x2, y2)
    xa1, ya1, xa2, ya2 = box_a
    xb1, yb1, xb2, yb2 = box_b
    inter_x1, inter_y1 = max(xa1, xb1), max(ya1, yb1)
    inter_x2, inter_y2 = min(xa2, xb2), min(ya2, yb2)
    inter_area = max(0, inter_x2 - inter_x1) * max(0, inter_y2 - inter_y1)
    area_a = (xa2 - xa1) * (ya2 - ya1)
    area_b = (xb2 - xb1) * (yb2 - yb1)
    return inter_area / (area_a + area_b - inter_area)

ground_truth_box = (50, 50, 150, 150)
# two very different predicted boxes, both correctly labeled as the right class
good_prediction_box = (55, 55, 145, 145)     # tight, accurate overlap
poor_prediction_box = (120, 120, 220, 220)   # barely overlaps the true object

good_iou = iou(ground_truth_box, good_prediction_box)
poor_iou = iou(ground_truth_box, poor_prediction_box)

iou_threshold = 0.5
good_counts_as_detection = good_iou >= iou_threshold
poor_counts_as_detection = poor_iou >= iou_threshold

# Try it yourself:
# print("IoU (good box):", good_iou, "-> counts as detection:", good_counts_as_detection)
# print("IoU (poor box):", poor_iou, "-> counts as detection:", poor_counts_as_detection)
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compute IoU and the counts-as-detection flag for both boxes at threshold 0.5, then try lowering the threshold to 0.3 and see whether the poor prediction now counts as a detection too - and think about what that implies for choosing an IoU threshold.

case_studies.title: Building a Classifier With Only 40 Labeled Images
case_studies.scenario: A team needs an image classifier for 5 product categories but only has about 40 labeled images per category. They plan to design and train a deep CNN from scratch, initializing all weights randomly.
case_studies.question: Given the data constraint, what approach is most likely to work meaningfully better than training a randomly-initialized CNN from scratch?

options.text: Design an even deeper CNN with more parameters
options.explanation: More parameters make a data-hungry model even hungrier for data. With only ~40 labeled examples per class, a bigger from-scratch network has even more capacity to overfit and even less chance of learning generalizable features from so few examples.

options.text: Use transfer learning: start from a network already trained on a large, general image dataset, and fine-tune only the last layer(s) on the small labeled set
options.explanation: A pretrained network has already learned general-purpose visual features (edges, textures, shapes) from a much larger dataset than the team has available. Reusing those features and only adapting the final layers to the 5 new categories requires far fewer new examples to work well than learning every feature from scratch on 40 images per class.

options.text: Use a larger batch size during training
options.explanation: Batch size affects the noisiness and speed of gradient updates, not the fundamental problem that there isn't enough labeled data to learn good visual features entirely from scratch.

options.text: Remove all regularization to let the model fit the data as closely as possible
options.explanation: Removing regularization would let the model fit the tiny training set even more closely, which increases overfitting risk rather than addressing the underlying scarcity of labeled data.

case_studies.key_takeaway: When labeled data is scarce, transfer learning from a model pretrained on a large, related dataset is usually far more effective than training a deep model from scratch, because it reuses already-learned general features instead of requiring the small dataset to teach the network everything.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming a deep learning problem always calls for a deep, from-scratch architecture, without considering whether there's enough data to actually learn one.

experimentation.objective: Approximate the effect of transfer learning versus training from scratch on the same very small labeled set - reusing a feature representation learned from more data should generalize much better than learning directly from 40 raw examples.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Simulate a labeled dataset (only a small slice of it is actually labeled)
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=400, n_features=200, n_informative=12,
                            n_redundant=0, n_classes=5, n_clusters_per_class=1,
                            class_sep=1.5, random_state=2)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=40, random_state=2)
# only 40 labeled training examples -- deliberately small, like the scenario

# "from scratch": train a classifier directly on raw high-dimensional features
scratch_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(X_train, y_train)

# "transfer learning" stand-in: reduce to a compact feature space fit on the FULL
# dataset (representing knowledge from a much larger pretraining set), then train
# only a simple classifier on top of those features using the small labeled set

X_train_transfer = pretrained_features.transform(X_train)
X_val_transfer = pretrained_features.transform(X_val)
transfer_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(X_train_transfer, y_train)

# Try it yourself:

# print("transfer-learning-style val accuracy:", transfer_model.score(X_val_transfer, y_val))

case_studies.title: The RNN That Forgets the Beginning of the Sentence
case_studies.scenario: A team trains a vanilla (non-gated) recurrent neural network on long text sequences, around 300-500 time steps per sequence, to predict a property of the whole sequence. The model performs reasonably when the answer depends mostly on the last few time steps, but performs poorly whenever the correct answer actually depends on information from very early in the sequence.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely explanation, and which class of architecture is designed to address it?

options.text: The hidden state size is too small - just increase the number of hidden units
options.explanation: A bigger hidden state gives the network more capacity per time step, but it doesn't change the fact that gradients (and the influence of early information) shrink multiplicatively as they propagate backward through hundreds of time steps - the core issue is about how far information and gradient can travel through time, not how much can be stored at each step.

options.text: Vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients over long sequences, since the same shrinking-derivative effect that occurs across deep layers also occurs across time steps; gated architectures like LSTM/GRU, or attention-based architectures like Transformers, are designed specifically to preserve long-range information
options.explanation: Backpropagation through time repeatedly multiplies gradients by the recurrent weight matrix and activation derivatives at every time step. Over hundreds of steps, this product typically shrinks toward zero, so information and gradient from early time steps barely influence the final prediction or the weight updates. LSTM/GRU gating mechanisms (and attention in Transformers, which connects distant time steps more directly) were designed specifically to preserve long-range dependencies that vanilla RNNs lose.

options.text: The learning rate needs to be increased
options.explanation: A larger learning rate doesn't restore information that has vanished from the gradient by the time it reaches early time steps - it would amplify whatever gradient signal is left, which is a very different problem than the signal not reaching there at all.

options.text: The model needs to be trained for many more epochs
options.explanation: More epochs of training with the same architecture and the same vanishing-gradient dynamics would not give early time steps meaningfully more influence over the loss - the structural limitation persists regardless of how long training continues.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Standard RNNs struggle to learn dependencies across long time gaps because gradients vanish as they backpropagate through many time steps, similar to how they vanish through many layers in a very deep feedforward network. Gated recurrent architectures (LSTM, GRU) and attention-based models (Transformers) exist largely to address this limitation.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming any RNN can learn arbitrarily long-range dependencies given enough hidden units or training time, without considering the structural vanishing-gradient limitation of the vanilla recurrent architecture itself.

experimentation.objective: See how the product of per-time-step gradient factors shrinks over a long sequence versus a short one, illustrating why information from early time steps barely reaches the end of a long sequence during backpropagation.

case_studies.title: The Rare-Disease Model That Never Says Yes
case_studies.scenario: A team trains a neural network to detect a rare disease from patient data, where only about 1% of patients in the training set actually have the disease. Trained with standard (unweighted) cross-entropy loss, the model converges to always predicting 'no disease' and still achieves 99% training accuracy.
case_studies.question: Which training-time technique most directly addresses this, beyond simply choosing a better evaluation metric?

options.text: Increase the learning rate
options.explanation: A different learning rate would change how quickly the model converges to some solution, but the '99% accuracy by always predicting no' solution is a genuinely low-loss point given unweighted cross-entropy on this class distribution - a different learning rate wouldn't stop the model from settling there.

options.text: Use a class-weighted loss (weighting the rare class more heavily in the cross-entropy calculation) or resample the training data (oversampling the rare class / undersampling the common class) so the model is actually penalized for missing the rare class
options.explanation: With unweighted cross-entropy, predicting 'no disease' for everyone is a strong (if useless) way to minimize loss when 99% of examples are actually negative. Weighting the loss so mistakes on the rare positive class cost more (or resampling so the training data isn't so lopsided) changes what the optimizer is actually incentivized to do, directly counteracting the collapse to the majority class.

options.text: Add more layers to the network
options.explanation: More capacity doesn't change the fact that, under the current loss function and class distribution, always predicting the majority class is already a very low-loss solution - a bigger model can find that same low-loss solution just as easily.

options.text: Increase the batch size only
options.explanation: Batch size affects the variance of gradient estimates, not the fundamental incentive structure created by an imbalanced, unweighted loss function - the majority-class collapse would likely still be the easiest low-loss solution regardless of batch size.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Under severe class imbalance, unweighted loss functions can make the majority-class-only prediction a genuinely low-loss solution, not just a lazy one. Class-weighted losses or resampling change the training incentive directly, rather than only changing how you measure the resulting model afterward.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating class imbalance purely as an evaluation-metric problem (which metric to report) without addressing that the training objective itself may be rewarding the majority-class collapse.

experimentation.objective: Train the same model with and without class weighting on an imbalanced synthetic dataset, and compare how well each one actually detects the rare class.

case_studies.title: BatchNorm on a Batch of Two
case_studies.scenario: A team training a 3D medical image segmentation model runs into GPU memory limits and can only fit a batch size of 2 per training step. They keep Batch Normalization layers as-is (as used in a tutorial trained with batch size 64). Training becomes unstable, and validation performance varies wildly between runs.
case_studies.question: What is the most likely contributor to this instability, and what's a reasonable fix?

options.text: Batch statistics (mean and variance) computed over a batch of only 2 examples are a very noisy estimate of the true population statistics, making BatchNorm's normalization unreliable; switching to Layer Normalization or Group Normalization, which don't depend on batch size, is a standard fix
options.explanation: BatchNorm normalizes each layer's activations using the mean and variance computed across the current batch. With only 2 examples, that estimate can vary enormously from batch to batch, injecting a lot of noise into every layer's normalization and destabilizing training. Layer Norm and Group Norm compute their statistics per-example (across channels/features rather than across the batch), so they remain stable regardless of batch size.

options.text: Just increase the learning rate to compensate
options.explanation: A higher learning rate would amplify whatever unstable, noisy signal is coming out of unreliable batch statistics, likely making the instability worse rather than better - it doesn't address why the normalization itself is noisy.

options.text: Remove all normalization layers entirely
options.explanation: Removing normalization entirely typically reintroduces the problems normalization was added to solve in the first place (e.g., unstable activation scales across layers) - the issue here is specifically that batch-based statistics are unreliable at this batch size, not that normalization in general is unhelpful.

options.text: Add more convolutional layers to the network
options.explanation: Adding more layers doesn't address why the normalization statistics computed from only 2 examples are noisy - it would just mean more layers are being fed an unreliable normalization signal.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Batch Normalization's reliability depends on having a large enough batch to estimate stable statistics. When memory constraints force very small batch sizes (common with large 3D or high-resolution inputs), batch-independent alternatives like Layer Norm or Group Norm are usually a better fit.
case_studies.common_misconception: Treating Batch Normalization as a drop-in default for any architecture and any batch size, without considering that its core assumption - a large enough batch to estimate reliable statistics - can break down under memory-constrained training.

experimentation.objective: Directly compare how noisy mean/variance estimates are from a tiny batch versus a larger batch, sampled repeatedly from the same underlying distribution.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
# assume activations across a layer are drawn from a fixed true distribution
true_mean, true_std = 2.0, 3.0
population = rng.normal(true_mean, true_std, size=100_000)

def batch_stats(batch_size, n_trials=10):
    estimates = []
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        batch = rng.choice(population, size=batch_size, replace=False)
        estimates.append((batch.mean(), batch.std()))
    return estimates

# Try it yourself:

# print("large batch estimates:", large_batch_estimates)

case_studies.title: The Text Generator That Blows Up Mid-Training
case_studies.scenario: A team training a recurrent network for text generation sees training proceed smoothly and losses decrease steadily for many epochs, then suddenly the loss jumps to an enormous value and becomes NaN within a couple of iterations, with no change to the learning rate or data.
case_studies.question: What is a standard technique specifically used to prevent this kind of sudden blow-up during RNN training?

options.text: Gradient clipping - capping the norm of the gradient before the weight update if it exceeds a chosen threshold
options.explanation: In recurrent networks, gradients are computed by backpropagating through many time steps, and if the recurrent weight matrix tends to amplify signals (the opposite of the vanishing-gradient case), the gradient can grow multiplicatively across time steps and occasionally spike to a huge value on some batches - exploding gradients. Clipping the gradient's norm to a maximum value before applying the update prevents any single step from taking a destructively large jump, without requiring a smaller learning rate overall.

options.text: Increase the model's depth
options.explanation: Adding more layers or a larger hidden state doesn't address why the gradient occasionally grows explosively across time steps during backpropagation - it would give the same exploding dynamic more places to occur, not fewer.

options.text: Increase the batch size
options.explanation: A larger batch changes how gradients are averaged across examples in a batch, but doesn't change the fact that backpropagation through many time steps within a single sequence can still produce an exploding gradient regardless of how many sequences are averaged together.

options.text: Remove all recurrent connections from the model
options.explanation: This would eliminate the network's ability to model sequential dependencies at all, rather than addressing the specific numerical instability - exploding gradients are a training stability issue with a much more targeted fix (clipping) than removing the architecture's core mechanism.

case_studies.key_takeaway: Exploding gradients - a sudden, large spike in gradient magnitude, often followed by NaN losses - are a common failure mode in recurrent networks trained on long sequences. Gradient clipping (capping the gradient norm before the update) is the standard, targeted fix, distinct from lowering the learning rate or changing the architecture.
case_studies.common_misconception: Confusing exploding gradients with vanishing gradients - they're opposite failure modes (gradient magnitude growing vs. shrinking across time steps or layers) with different standard fixes (clipping vs. non-saturating activations/gating).

experimentation.objective: See how a per-step gradient factor slightly greater than 1 compounds into an enormous value over many time steps, and how clipping bounds the result.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
sequence_length = 50
# per-step Jacobian norms slightly greater than 1 (e.g. recurrent weight matrix norm > 1)
per_step_gradient_norms = rng.normal(loc=1.15, scale=0.05, size=sequence_length)

raw_gradient_magnitude = np.prod(per_step_gradient_norms)  # compounds -> explodes

def clip_gradient(grad, max_norm=5.0):
    return min(grad, max_norm)

clipped_gradient_magnitude = clip_gradient(raw_gradient_magnitude, max_norm=5.0)

# Try it yourself:
# print("raw (unclipped) gradient magnitude after 50 steps:", raw_gradient_magnitude)
# print("gradient magnitude after clipping:", clipped_gradient_magnitude)
# # try reducing sequence_length to 10 and see how much smaller the unclipped value becomes
experimentation.suggested_exploration: Compare raw_gradient_magnitude to clipped_gradient_magnitude, then reduce sequence_length to 10 and recompute raw_gradient_magnitude to see how much smaller it is over a shorter sequence - the same mechanism, just compounded over fewer steps.

case_studies.title: The Fraud Model With 'Perfect' Probabilities
case_studies.scenario: A fraud model has a strong ROC-AUC of 0.94. The risk team now wants to use its predicted probability directly as an expected-loss estimate: a transaction scored 0.80 should contain roughly 80% fraud risk among similar transactions. When they bucket predictions, transactions predicted at 0.8 are fraudulent only about 0.35 of the time, and those predicted at 0.2 are fraudulent about 0.08 of the time.
case_studies.question: What should the team investigate or fix before using the model's probabilities to make expected-cost decisions?

options.text: Increase the ROC-AUC further; a higher AUC guarantees better probability estimates
options.explanation: ROC-AUC measures ranking quality: whether positives tend to receive higher scores than negatives. A model can rank cases extremely well while its numerical probabilities are badly calibrated.

options.text: Calibrate the model's predicted probabilities on separate validation data, using a method such as Platt scaling or isotonic regression
options.explanation: The observed frequencies differ substantially from the predicted probabilities, which is a calibration problem. Calibration methods learn a mapping from the model's raw scores to probabilities that better match observed event frequencies. Calibration should be performed on data not used to fit the original model.

options.text: Convert every probability to a hard 0/1 prediction before computing expected cost
options.explanation: Hard labels throw away the probability information the risk team explicitly wants to use. The problem is that the probabilities are not trustworthy as probabilities, not that probabilities should be discarded.

options.text: Use accuracy instead of ROC-AUC because accuracy directly measures probability quality
options.explanation: Accuracy evaluates thresholded class decisions and says nothing about whether a predicted 0.8 corresponds to an 80% event frequency. It is not a calibration metric.

case_studies.key_takeaway: A model can discriminate well and still be poorly calibrated. When predicted probabilities themselves drive pricing, reserves, triage, or expected-cost decisions, calibration must be evaluated and, when needed, corrected separately from ranking metrics.
case_studies.common_misconception: Assuming a high ROC-AUC means a model's probability values can automatically be interpreted literally.

experimentation.objective: Create a classifier whose scores rank examples well but whose predicted probabilities are systematically overconfident, then compare a reliability diagram and calibration error before and after calibration.
